segments.title: How Age of Sail ratings counted guns
segments.summary: First-, second-, and third-rate Age of Sail warships were grouped by gun count because similar weapons made the total a useful guide to fighting power.
segments.body: Labels such as 74 and 80 describe ships by their total number of guns. A first rate carried at least 100 guns. Second rates fell around 86 to 90 guns, while third rates ran from about 64 to 84. These bands worked because the weapons being counted were comparable enough for the total to indicate a ship's relative fighting power. As guns diverged in power and purpose, that shorthand became less useful.

evidence.note: The transcript outlines first, second, and third rates by gun totals.

segments.title: Why modern gun totals became misleading
segments.summary: Modern gun totals lost much of their value once calibre, shell effects, range, and accuracy determined what a few weapons could achieve.
segments.body: Individual weapons became much more powerful and specialised. A 1930s sloop armed with only two or three 4-inch guns is compared with both fleets at the Battle of Trafalgar. In this imagined encounter, high-explosive shells, longer effective range, and accurate fire would make most targets single-shot kills. A small modern gun count can therefore represent far more combat power than a large Age of Sail total. Counting barrels says little once the weapons and their effects are no longer broadly comparable.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts a 1930s sloop's few modern guns with earlier fleets.

segments.title: Why the main battery defines a modern warship
segments.summary: For a modern warship, its role and principal battery, such as 6-inch or 8-inch cruiser guns, reveal more than a total that mixes many weapon types.
segments.body: A World War II warship might carry main guns, 40 mm and 20 mm weapons, and machine guns, so its headline total would mix weapons with very different jobs. In a ship-to-ship gunnery duel, the main battery usually supplies the meaningful topline figure. Lighter weapons remain important against aircraft, motor torpedo boats, and targets at very close range because those situations call for different capabilities. Historians therefore describe a cruiser by role and principal calibre, for example as a 6-inch or 8-inch cruiser. The wording is longer than an Age of Sail rating because it preserves distinctions that one gun total would hide.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes main 6-inch or 8-inch batteries from lighter weapons and their roles.

segments.title: Why modern warship labels are wordier
segments.summary: A dramatic total such as 90 guns can mislead when many of those weapons are machine guns with little bearing on a ship-to-ship gunnery duel.
segments.body: First-, second-, and third-rate labels were concise. Modern classification needs more words to describe combat capability accurately. The television example asks whether a ship can simply be described as carrying 90 guns. That total hides the fact that roughly 50 could be machine guns, which contribute little to a ship-to-ship gunnery duel. A role and main-battery description is less elegant and identifies the weapons that matter for the comparison being made.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that a television-friendly total can count about 50 machine guns that do not matter in a ship-to-ship gunnery duel.
